replacement: I should not have chosen to live in a republic of recent founding, however excellent its laws. I should have feared that the government, perhaps framed differently from what the circumstances of the moment required, might not suit the new citizens, or they might not suit it, and that the State would risk overthrow and destruction almost as soon as it came into being. For liberty is like those solid and succulent foods, or those generous wines, that nourish and strengthen robust constitutions used to them, but ruin and intoxicate weak and delicate constitutions not suited to them. Peoples once accustomed to masters are unable to do without them. If they try to shake off the yoke, they only estrange themselves further from freedom. They mistake for freedom an unbridled license that is its exact opposite, and almost always, through their revolutions, they deliver themselves to seducers who make their chains heavier than before. The Roman people itself, a model for all free peoples, was wholly incapable of governing itself when it escaped the oppression of the Tarquins. It had been debased by slavery and by the ignominious tasks imposed on it, and at first it was no better than a stupid mob, which had to be controlled and governed with the greatest wisdom. Only so could it grow accustomed, by degrees, to breathe the health-giving air of liberty, and its minds, enervated or rather brutalized under tyranny, might gradually acquire that severity of morals and spirit of fortitude which would finally make it the most respectable of all peoples. I should, then, have looked for a peaceful and happy Republic as my country, one of such antiquity that it was lost, as it were, in the night of time. It would have suffered only such shocks as served to show and strengthen the courage and patriotism of its subjects. Its citizens, long accustomed to a wise independence, would have been not only free but worthy to be so.

May a Republic so wisely and happily constituted last for ever, as an example to other nations and for the felicity of its own citizens! This is the only prayer you have left to make, the only precaution that remains to be taken. For the future it depends on yourselves alone (not to make you happy, for your ancestors have saved you that trouble), but to make that happiness lasting, by your wisdom in enjoying it. Your preservation depends on your constant union, your obedience to the laws and your respect for their ministers. If the smallest trace of bitterness or distrust remains among you, hasten to destroy it, as an accursed leaven that sooner or later must bring misfortune and ruin on the State. I conjure you all to look into your hearts and to hearken to the secret voice of conscience. Can any of you find, throughout the universe, a more upright, more enlightened and more honorable body than your magistracy? Do not all its members set you an example of moderation, of simplicity of manners, of respect for the laws and of the most sincere harmony? Place, therefore, without reserve, that salutary confidence in such wise superiors which reason ever owes to virtue. Consider that they are your own choice, that they justify that choice, and that the honors due to those you have dignified are necessarily yours by reflection. Not one of you is so ignorant as not to know that when the laws lose their force, and those who defend them lose their authority, security and liberty are universally impossible. Why, then, should you hesitate to do cheerfully and with just confidence what your true interest, your duty and reason itself would have bound you to do all along?

And you, most honorable and magnificent lords, the worthy and revered magistrates of a free people, permit me to offer you in particular my duty and homage. If there is a station in the world that can confer honor on those who fill it, it is undoubtedly the one that virtue and talents combine to bestow, the one you have made yourselves worthy of and to which your fellow-citizens have raised you. Their worth adds a new luster to your own. You have been chosen, by men capable of governing others, to govern themselves, and so I cannot but hold you as much superior to all other magistrates as a free people, and particularly the one over which you have the honor to preside, is superior by its wisdom and its reason to the populace of other States.

We cannot see without surprise and disgust how little agreement there is among the authors who have treated this great subject. Among the more important writers there are scarcely two of the same mind. I say nothing of the ancient philosophers, who seem to have done their best to contradict one another on the most fundamental principles. The Roman jurists subjected man and the other animals indiscriminately to the same natural law, because they took that name to mean the law that nature imposes on herself rather than the law she prescribes to others. Or rather, it was because of the particular sense the term law has among those jurists, who seem on this occasion to have understood by it only the general relations nature establishes between all animated beings for their common preservation. The moderns understand by the term law merely a rule prescribed to a moral being, that is to say, to a being who is intelligent and free and is considered in his relations to other beings. They therefore confine the jurisdiction of natural law to man, as the only animal endowed with reason. But each defines this law after his own fashion, and they have founded it on such metaphysical principles that very few among us can understand them, much less discover them for ourselves. So the definitions of these learned men, which differ in everything else, agree only in this: it is impossible to understand the law of nature, and consequently to obey it, without being a very subtle casuist and a profound metaphysician. All of which is as much as to say that mankind, in establishing society, must have used a capacity that is acquired only with great difficulty, and by very few persons, even in a state of society.

Every animal has ideas, since it has senses, and it even combines those ideas to some degree. Man differs from the brute in this only by degree. Some philosophers have even maintained that there is a greater difference between one man and another than between some men and some beasts. So what sets man apart from the brute in kind is not so much understanding as the human quality of free-agency. Nature commands every animal, and the brute obeys. Man feels the same impulse, but knows he is at liberty to yield or to resist. It is above all in his consciousness of this liberty that the spirituality of his soul shows itself. Physics can explain, in some measure, how the senses work and how ideas form. But in the power of willing, or rather of choosing, and in the feeling of that power, we find only acts that are purely spiritual and that the laws of mechanism cannot explain at all.

Still, the difficulties that surround all these questions might leave room to dispute whether men and brutes differ in this way. There is another very specific quality that distinguishes them, and about it there can be no dispute. It is the faculty of self-improvement. Helped by circumstances, it gradually develops all our other faculties, and it belongs to the species as it does to the individual. A brute is, after a few months, all that he will ever be in his whole life, and his species after a thousand years is exactly what it was in the first year of that thousand. Why is man alone liable to become a dotard? Is it not because he returns, in this, to his primitive state? The brute has acquired nothing and so has nothing to lose, and it keeps the force of instinct. Man loses, through age or accident, all that his perfectibility had enabled him to gain, and so sinks lower than the brutes themselves. It would be melancholy to be forced to admit that this distinctive and almost unlimited faculty is the source of all human misfortunes. It would be melancholy to admit that it draws man, in time, out of his original state, in which he would have passed his days insensibly in peace and innocence. It would be melancholy to admit that this faculty, producing in successive ages his discoveries and his errors, his vices and his virtues, makes him at length a tyrant over himself and over nature.[1] It would be shocking to have to regard as a benefactor the man who first suggested to the Oroonoko Indians the use of the boards they apply to the temples of their children, which secure to them some part at least of their weakness and original happiness.

Men in a state of nature are confined to what is physical in love. They are fortunate enough to be ignorant of those excellences which sharpen the appetite while they make it harder to satisfy. They must therefore be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and so they fall into fewer and less violent quarrels. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages. They quietly await the impulses of nature and yield to them involuntarily, with more pleasure than ardor; and once their wants are satisfied, the desire is gone. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all the other passions, must have acquired in society that glowing impetuosity which so often makes it fatal to mankind. It is all the more absurd to portray savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribeans, who have so far deviated least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable of people in their love affairs and the least subject to jealousy, though they live in a hot climate which seems always to inflame the passions.

Let us conclude, then, that man in a state of nature has no industry, no speech and no home, but wanders up and down the forests. He is as much a stranger to war as to every tie. He has no need of his fellow creatures and no desire to harm them, and perhaps does not even tell one from another. Let us conclude also that, being self-sufficient and subject to so few passions, he could have only such feelings and knowledge as befitted his situation. He felt only his actual necessities. He paid no attention to anything he did not think himself immediately concerned to notice, and his understanding advanced no further than his vanity. If he happened to make a discovery, he was the less able to pass it on, because he did not even know his own children. Every art would necessarily die with its inventor, where men had no kind of education and generation followed generation without the least advance. All started from the same point, and so centuries must have gone by in the barbarism of the first ages; the race was already old, and man remained a child.

Ideas and feelings followed one another, and heart and head came into play. Men went on laying aside their original wildness, and their private connections grew more intimate every day as their limits widened. They got used to gathering before their huts round a large tree. Singing and dancing, the true offspring of love and leisure, became the amusement, or rather the occupation, of the men and women who gathered there with nothing else to do. Each began to consider the rest and to wish to be considered in turn. Thus public esteem came to carry a value. The best singer or dancer, the handsomest, the strongest, the most dexterous or the most eloquent, came to be the most considered. This was the first step toward inequality, and at the same time toward vice. These first distinctions gave rise to vanity and contempt on the one side, and to shame and envy on the other. The fermentation caused by these new leavens ended by producing combinations fatal to innocence and happiness.

How men first came to know and use iron is hard to conjecture. We cannot suppose they would of themselves think of digging ore out of a mine and preparing it for smelting before they knew what would come of it. Nor have we much reason to suppose some accidental fire made the discovery, since mines form only in barren places, bare of trees and plants. It looks as if nature had taken pains to keep the fatal secret from us. Only the extraordinary accident of a volcano remains. By throwing out metallic substances already in fusion, it suggested to the onlookers the idea of imitating what nature did. We must also conceive them as having uncommon courage and foresight, to undertake so laborious a work with so distant a prospect of advantage. Yet such qualities are found together only in minds more advanced than we can suppose those of the first discoverers to have been.

In this state of affairs, equality could have been kept up if individuals had had equal talents, and if, for example, the use of iron and the consumption of commodities had always balanced exactly. But nothing kept this balance, and it was soon upset. The strongest did the most work; the most skilful made the best use of his labor; the most ingenious found ways to lessen his labor. The husbandman needed more iron, or the smith more corn. Both labored equally, yet one gained a great deal by his work while the other could hardly support himself. So natural inequality unfolds itself gradually together with that of combination. As circumstances differ, the differences between men develop; they grow more noticeable and more lasting in their effects, and they begin to influence the lot of individuals in the same proportion.

With this aim, he first described to his neighbors the horror of a situation that armed every man against the rest, made their possessions as burdensome to them as their wants, and offered no safety either in riches or in poverty. Then he easily devised plausible arguments to bring them round to his design. "Let us join together," he said, "to protect the weak from oppression, to hold the ambitious in check, and to secure for every man what belongs to him. Let us set up rules of justice and peace, which all without exception may be bound to obey. These rules may make up in some measure for the caprices of fortune, by subjecting the powerful and the weak alike to reciprocal obligations. In a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, let us gather them into a supreme power that will govern us by wise laws, protect and defend all the members of the association, drive off our common enemies, and maintain eternal harmony among us."

I know that some writers have given other accounts of the origin of political societies, such as the conquest of the powerful or the association of the weak. It makes no difference to my argument which of these causes we choose. Still, the one I have just laid down appears to me the most natural, for the following reasons. First, in the case of conquest, the right of conquest is no right in itself, so it could not serve as a foundation for any other. The victor and the vanquished remained in a state of war toward each other, unless the vanquished were restored to the full possession of their liberty and freely chose the victor as their chief. Until then, whatever capitulation had been made was founded on violence and therefore ipso facto void. On this hypothesis, there could have been neither a real society or body politic nor any law other than that of the strongest. Second, in the case of the association of the weak, the words strong and weak are ambiguous. In the interval between the establishment of a right of property, or prior occupancy, and that of political government, the meaning of these words is better expressed by the terms rich and poor. For before laws existed, men had no other way of subjecting their equals than by attacking their goods or by handing over some of their own goods to them. Third, the poor had nothing to lose but their freedom. It would have been utterly absurd for them to give up voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed, and to get nothing in exchange. The rich, on the other hand, had feelings, if I may so express myself, in every part of their possessions. It was therefore much easier to harm them, and more necessary for them to take precautions against harm. In short, it is more reasonable to suppose that a thing was invented by those it would serve than by those it must have harmed.

If we reflect on this subject with even a little attention, we shall find new arguments to confirm this truth, and we shall be convinced from the very nature of the contract that it cannot be irrevocable. Suppose there were no superior power capable of ensuring the fidelity of the contracting parties or of compelling them to perform their reciprocal engagements. Then the parties would be sole judges in their own cause, and each would always have a right to renounce the contract as soon as he found that the other had violated its terms, or that they no longer suited his convenience. It is on this principle that the right of abdication may possibly be founded. Now, if we consider here only what is human in this institution, it is certain that, if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and appropriates to himself all the advantages of the contract, has none the less a right to renounce his authority, the people, who suffer for all the faults of their chief, must have a much better right to renounce their dependence. But the terrible and innumerable quarrels and disorders that would necessarily arise from so dangerous a privilege show, more than anything else, how much human governments needed a more solid basis than mere reason. They show how expedient it was for the public tranquillity that the divine will should step in to invest the sovereign authority with a sacred and inviolable character, which might deprive subjects of the fatal right of disposing of it. If the world had received no other advantages from religion, this would be enough to impose on men the duty of adopting and cultivating it, abuses and all, since it has saved more blood than fanaticism has ever spilled. But let us follow the thread of our hypothesis.
